title: Using your personal phone for work: What it costs you
summary: Learn about how much using a personal phone for work actually costs, what your employer can and can't see, and how to separate work from personal calls.
body_markdown:
Do you run a business and use your personal phone for work calls? Maybe you’re a new employee who’s just joined a small business. When you’re starting a new role, either as founder or employee, you’re faced with the same question: should I use my personal device for work calls?


You’re not alone. Small businesses have started adopting[Bring Your Own Device](https://www.quo.com/blog/byod-policy/) , or BYOD, policies as remote and hybrid work has grown. Under BYOD, employees use personal devices, such as cell phones or laptops, instead of[company hardware](https://www.quo.com/blog/company-cell-phones/) .


BYOD is now common for modern businesses. A 2022 survey from Samsung and Oxford Economics found[only 15%](https://insights.samsung.com/2022/04/18/smartphones-and-your-employees-to-byod-or-not-to-byod/) of small- to medium-sized businesses provide devices to all employees. That leaves most employees downloading[Slack and taking work calls](https://www.quo.com/features/slack-voip) from their personal phones and laptops.


But you might be wondering: is using a personal phone for work legal?


Using a personal phone for work is legal, and for a lot of people it’s more convenient than carrying a second device. However, the costs of using a personal cell number for work show up later:


- **You lose privacy.** Your personal number ends up in customers’ phones permanently, so calls can arrive at any hour.
- **You can’t easily separate work and personal calls.** When a call comes in, you don’t know how to respond. You have to find out who’s calling before responding to them appropriately.
- **More difficult to shut off work.** Instead of giving up your personal number at your workplace, use a separate work number on your existing device. We’ll dive into this topic below and offer better options to help you maintain your work-life balance.


*Note:* *Keep in mind that none of what we’ve shared here should be taken as legal advice. You should double-check tax and legal requirements with an accountant and a lawyer.*


##


**Using a personal phone for work vs using a business phone**


Aside from using your personal *number,* using your personal phone rather than a work phone issued by your employer has its pros and cons. Let’s take a look:


Using a personal phone for work Using a business phone for work


Convenience Only one device to carry Requires carrying two devices


Privacy Risk of exposing personal data to an employer Personal data stays private


Security Must comply with work profiles or mobile device management apps Pre-configured with company security to protect confidential information


Work-life balance Harder to separate work and personal life Clear separation between work and personal life


Cost per employee for businesses $15–$50 per month, assuming they’re using a business phone provider $200–$500+


Control over business contacts Employee can add, edit, and remove contacts Employee can edit contact data, but employer has visibility


On the positive side, using personal cell phones for work means you don’t have to[carry an extra phone](https://www.quo.com/blog/carrying-two-phones/) . You can manage everything on one device, including the second number you use for work. You also have the freedom to use whatever device you prefer. With your personal phone, you already have a device with settings that match your preferences, instead of setting up a new one from scratch. And when you move on from your company, you won’t have to schedule a device handoff.


For employers, having personal phones in the workplace reduces bottom-line expenses. You don’t need to purchase new phones and pay for monthly cell lines.


However, using your own mobile phone for work has some drawbacks.


Some businesses have strict company policies and security protocols surrounding customer and company data. To mitigate cybersecurity risks, they’ll install a work profile on Android phones. They might also install a mobile device management, or MDM, app on iOS devices to ensure the security of their corporate data.


Alternatively, your employer may ask you to connect to your company’s virtual private network to conduct business remotely.


Either scenario can expose your personal data, including your contacts, photos, texts, and social media interactions, to your employer. And yes, this is legal.


But you don’t have to worry about these drawbacks. You can still take advantage of a BYOD policy without risking employee privacy. The solution: using a separate business number with personal phones.


##


3 Reasons why entrepreneurs and teams should avoid using personal phone numbers for work


Whether you’re the founder of a company or an employee, using your personal device as a company phone can be convenient. But if you’re considering using your personal cell phone number as your work number, you may want to think twice. Here’s why.


### **1. Disruption of work-life balance**


[Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/breaking-down-infinite-workday) found that 40% of people online at 6 a.m. are reviewing email to set the day’s priorities, and the pattern repeats at night. By 10 p.m., 29% of active workers are back in their inboxes. Chats sent outside the standard 9-to-5 window are up 15% year over year, averaging 58 messages per person before or after hours. That includes the first thing in the morning, in the evening, and on weekends.


This constant blurring of work-life boundaries can lead to[chronic fatigue, stress, and burnout](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8782676/) . And once you give coworkers and clients your personal phone number, you can’t take it back.


If you work for a global organization that spans multiple time zones, using a personal phone may mean you receive calls or texts at all hours. And unless you stick to strict business hours while working from home or silence your phone, your personal and home life could suffer.


### **2. Difficulty keeping work and personal calls separate**


When everyone uses the same phone number to call you, it becomes impossible to distinguish between personal and work-related calls. You never know what “hat” you need to wear until you pick up the phone. When you accidentally pick up a client call when you thought you were answering the pizza delivery guy, it’s hard to hang up politely. Inadvertently answering a work call in the wrong context might come off as unprofessional to your client or manager.


Another side effect of using your personal number to make work calls is having work and personal contacts in your address book. Texts and voicemails from customers and coworkers become mixed with your personal SMS and MMS messages and missed calls.


It’s easy to see how critical work-related messages could slip through the cracks. And while the occasional missed call or text might not seem like the end of the world, for many customers, that’s all it takes. According to Zendesk’s Trends Report,[one in two customers](https://www.zendesk.com/blog/what-is-bad-customer-service/) will switch to a competitor after a single negative support experience.


### **3. Loss of privacy**


Sharing your personal phone number is like letting a genie out of a bottle. There’s no pushing it back in, unless you get a new phone number.


What might have been an act of good faith to your entire personal client roster may affect you for years to come. You could say “Reach out anytime!” only for customers to call you at all hours of the day. Imagine continuing to receive business-related calls from those contacts long after you change employers.


This loss of privacy also comes with legitimate security concerns. Sharing your personal phone number can make it easier for individuals to find your current or past home addresses, social media profiles, and the full names of your family members or friends. If your personal phone number falls into the wrong hands, it can expose you to[phishing, scams, or identity theft](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-recognize-avoid-phishing-scams) .


##


What MDM software can and can’t see


**


MDM refers to software tools that allow businesses to monitor employee activity on their work devices. They can be remotely installed on computers and smartphones. Employers use MDM tools to remotely configure employee devices, control access to company applications, and remotely wipe company data if needed. This helps reduce data breaches and leaks related to sensitive information.


However, over the past decade, companies have turned to more invasive MDM tools known as ‘bossware.’ These tools can take periodic screenshots of an employee’s device. They can also record which apps employees use on their devices. If you’re using a personal phone for work, these tools can see if you’re using social media apps and can log your activity as well.


*Source:*[Electronic Frontier Foundation](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/06/inside-invasive-secretive-bossware-tracking-workers)


Small businesses don’t typically invest in MDM software to manage employee devices. However, you should be clear about company expectations when employees agree to use personal phones for work. If you’re running a company, you want to know what team members are talking about with customers. But you don’t need to micromanage all communications on their device. That can lead to a poor work experience and reduce team morale over time.

##


How to ask for a separate business number from your company


If your business has a BYOD policy, here’s how you can make the case to get a separate business number:


- **Sharing incoming calls and texts during business hours.** Show your manager how virtual phone apps like Quo can ring team members simultaneously. That can help reduce missed calls. Plus, a shared text inbox lets team members jump into text conversations together. It can help improve your first response times.
- **Visibility into customer conversations.** A separate business number from a virtual phone provider gives your team access to every conversation. Emphasize the importance of shared context to support lead conversion and customer service.
- **Maintaining client relationships.** Let businesses know the risk they face when you move on to another company. Their customer contacts and client relationships will sit in your phone, and they might not be able to continue those relationships.


Another argument is that using your personal phone for work can lead to reimbursement expenses for the business. Keep in mind: no federal law requires employees to use their personal phones for work or mandates that employers reimburse business-related phone expenses.


That said,[some states](https://www.shouselaw.com/ca/blog/do-i-get-reimbursed-for-business-use-of-my-personal-cell-phone/#_edn2) require employers to reimburse employees for business-related phone expenses. That includes California, Illinois, Iowa, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, and the District of Columbia. These states allow employers to set their own policies for reimbursing personal cell phone use, as long as their rules comply with state law.


If you’re in a state without such laws, whether you can refuse to use your personal phone depends on your company’s policies and willingness to provide alternatives, such as a work phone or a stipend. Many employers are open to covering a portion of your phone bill, especially if you ask to[add a virtual business phone number](https://www.quo.com/blog/get-virtual-phone-number/) to your personal device. A virtual business phone number will let you keep your work number separate from your personal line and comes with a set monthly cost.


Of course, if you’re self-employed or reimbursing employees, you can also write off[cell phone use as a business expense](https://turbotax.intuit.com/tax-tips/small-business-taxes/can-cellphone-expenses-be-tax-deductible-with-a-business/L6NQvycMO) per the IRS. W-2 employees generally cannot deduct unreimbursed business expenses.


##


Final verdict: Should you use your personal phone for work?


If you’re an employee, using your personal phone for work may be fine for a while. But it’s not sustainable if you want to maintain work-life balance and protect your privacy.


If you’re an employer, having a BYOD policy can reduce your monthly phone expenses. But avoid having your team use their personal numbers for customer communications. You risk losing your client relationships and your shared conversation history.


A separate work number on each person’s existing phone solves these two challenges without buying anyone a second device. **FAQs**


**Does an employer have to pay for their employee’s cell phone?**


It depends on your location; some states, like California and Illinois, require reimbursement for business-related phone expenses, but no federal law mandates it.


**Can I refuse to use my personal phone for work?**


The short answer is it depends on your situation and where you live.


Some states require employers to reimburse employees for business-related phone expenses. If your employer chooses to deny reimbursement, you could make a case for having a separate work phone to make business calls.


**How do I calculate a cell phone reimbursement?**


You can calculate a cell phone reimbursement in two ways:
**1. Flat monthly stipend.** Propose a stipend between $40–$70 depending on your monthly phone bill. Pitch an amount based on how phone-intensive your role is.
**2. Percentage basis.** If your monthly phone expenses depend on how many minutes you pay for, you can calculate your work-related calls and invoice your employer accordingly.


With a virtual phone system like Quo, you get access to unlimited calls and texts for every number in your account. You can skip the reimbursement process and just pay for your virtual number every month. Save time for both your employees and your finance team.


**How do I separate work and personal data on my phone?**


Adding a virtual business number, like Quo, creates a clear separation by keeping work communication in a dedicated app. This allows you to manage personal and business calls on one device without mixing them.


**Does a work profile mean my employer can see my personal apps?**


It depends on what MDM software your employer installs on your device. Quo isn’t MDM software, so we don’t have access to a device’s personal information. Quo apps don’t give employers access to their employees’ personal apps.
